title: Teaching Information
text:
I am a strong believer that any student can learn from the right teacher. I have had many, many conversations with students whose biggest struggle often comes down to a disconnect between the teacher (or professor) and the student. The relationship between students and teachers often times reminds me of Plato’s The Cave. The teacher is trying to introduce the student to the teacher’s world, but the student is viewing the teacher’s world through the lens of the student’s own understanding of the world. Each step is a breach into the student’s understanding of the world, and the wrong guide may struggle to help them. Additionally, my experience in teaching has taught me that the teacher is also only capable of interpreting the world from their own perspective, and the student is also attempting to introduce the teacher into the student’s view of the world. Perhaps that is just an analogy for communication in general, but it resonates with me as an apt way to describe the difficulty in being both the teacher and the student. Both are captives to their own perspectives.
We cannot meet the needs of every student, and we cannot force every student to put in effort, but we can make a difference.

title: Choosing a Programming Language
text:
Python is my language of choice. In my opinion, choosing a language to start learning how to operate in is much less important than simply starting to learn. Going between different programming languages requires learning new words, sure, but the logic behind how computers handle information does not vary wildly. The logic behind computer science is essentially a form of math, and logical concepts such as multiplication and addition both work just fine even if we change bases or how we represent them.
Example:
Python makes a lot of assumptions for you. If you want to store a number to use later, you simply tell it: x = 5, and it will run that no problem. Python sees a whole number on its own and assumes that it is an integer1. It handles the memory and background categorization for you.
C does not make the same assumptions that Python does. If you put x = 5 into C, it will break. C assumes nothing about what x is supposed to be, so it doesn’t know how much memory to give it. You need to explicitly tell it that x is an integer by writing int x = 5;, and it will handle it no problem.
The logic of storing and manipulating data is a simple process, but the language used to describe it changes. Learning the logic of computers is often the hardest part for people, and transitioning to another language after that is not nearly as difficult. That being said, choosing a language to begin with often goes hand-in-hand with what you want to accomplish.



Python
+ Industry standard for AI, machine learning, and data science
+ Excellent data handling/analysis ability (uses packages that run highly optimized C/Fortran code in the background)
+ Very beginner-friendly
+ Makes lots of assumptions (handles memory for you)
+ Tons of useful packages created by others
- Slow execution speed
- Whitespace matters
- Can hide the inner workings, making performance issues harder to debug
- Makes lots of assumptions (less manual control) 


C or C++
+ Unmatched processing speed and precise memory control
+ Can run on pretty much every piece of hardware
+ Industry standard for systems programming and hardware integration
+ C++ in particular is the standard for game development (Unreal Engine)
- Complex syntax
- Need to understand manual memory handling
- Assumes very little (you have to build everything explicitly) 


Fortran
+ Extremely fast and efficient for heavy numerical arrays and complex math
+ Tons of use in scientific computing and supercomputing
+ Can explicitly manage memory handling
+ Decades and decades of optimized math libraries to pull from 
- Super old
- Need to explicitly understand memory handling
- Not suited for general-purpose programming or modern UX 


Java and C#
+ Industry standards for massive corporate application development
+ Highly general-purpose (they power everything from mobile apps to heavy enterprise servers)
+ Object-oriented, making them scalable for large teams
+ C# for game development (Unity) 
- Syntax is verbose (requires a lot of boilerplate code)
- Can have slower startup times and higher memory overhead than C/C++ 


Javascript / Typescript
+ Industry standard for web development
+ Runs natively in web browsers
+ Full-stack development possible (one language for front-end and back-end)
+ Massive industry and community
+ TypeScript adds strict rules (types) to prevent messy errors in large projects
- Large, complex dependency trees
- Vanilla JavaScript can be prone to runtime errors 


Rust and Go
+ Industry standard for Web3, microservices, and modern cloud infrastructure
+ Rust can be extremely fast (comparable to C) and guarantees memory safety
+ Go is designed to be easy to learn and handles thousands of simultaneous tasks effortlessly 
- Rust is notoriously difficult to learn
- Go syntax is extremely verbose (requires writing repetitive code because it lacks certain advanced features) 



Do you want to work in data analysis or AI? Choose Python. Do you want to work in game development? Choose either C++ or C#. Do you want to delve into the ins and outs of how a computer handles information? Choose C. Do you want to be able to hang with all of the old computational physicists and complain about how slow Python is? Choose Fortran. Do you want to become a full-stack or web developer? Choose Javascript/Typescript. Do you want to make a phone app? Choose Java. Rust and Go are so new that I honestly don’t know much about them, but if you want to dive into those new territories, go for it!
If you don’t know what you want to do yet, then I’ll make it simple for you. Just start with Python.

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
The term bit is short for binary digit . It is a system that exists in one of two states: 0 or 1, which gives us the “bi-” in binary .
If you are inquisitive, you might ask, “Why exactly 0 and 1?” The truth is, the specific numbers don’t matter as long as we choose exactly two states and stay consistent . For example, physical computer circuits look for two voltage inputs: 0V or 5V . That is still a binary system. We represent bits as 0 or 1 purely for mathematical simplicity .


In daily life, the number 0 is often associated with “nothing” or “off.” By contrast, 1 is clearly “not zero,” representing “something” or “on” .
If I asked you, “Is there a dog in your room?” and your answer was “no”, that corresponds to 0 dogs . If your answer was “yes”, that corresponds to at least 1 dog . By this logic, 0 represents the absence of something, and 1 represents the presence of something . This is the heart of a bit’s simplicity .
Why does it have to be binary? Why not ternary (0, 1, 2) or quaternary (0, 1, 2, 3)?  The simplest way to evaluate reality is to ask a fundamental question: Does this exist, or not?  There is little room for confusion because both the question and the answer are absolute . This absolute simplicity is vital when we want to stack millions of these questions together to build complex computational structures .

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
What is a Bit, Really?
Calling a bit a “binary digit” doesn’t actually explain its physical nature . A bit is actually a single unit of information .
There is an entire field of science called Information Theory that has been evolving for over 160 years . The accelerating technological advancements we have seen since WWII run parallel to breakthroughs in this field . (If you have heard of quantum computers, they rely on qubits, which are simply the quantum mechanical version of bits used in Quantum Information Theory ).
In 1867, a famous physicist named James Clerk Maxwell proposed a thought experiment—known as Maxwell’s Demon—to test the second law of thermodynamics . The pursuit of resolving this physics puzzle eventually led scientists to a profound realization: Information is a real, physical quantity . Just as you measure distance in meters, you measure information in bits .

Representing Information
To exchange or store information, we must encode it into a physical medium .
Picture someone using a flashlight to transmit messages in Morse code . The photons coming from the flashlight do not inherently possess special properties that carry data . Yet, communication happens because we encode information into the existence (1) and nonexistence (0) of those photons .
Let’s make a single bit equal to a single unit of Morse code time. Here is how a message might look:

010100000001011101010001110111011100010101011100010000000111010111000101110001011101000101110001110111011100011101011100010

This sequence translates to “I love karaoke” . Sending that specific pattern required 123 bits .
Does this mean the literal concept of loving karaoke has a physical mass of 123 bits? No . The bits do not hold semantic meaning; they only hold the structure of the message . If I send the word “love” to 100 people, it means 100 different things. The scientific information contained in those bits is just the structural arrangement of the word itself, not human emotion .


Information and Entropy
In the early 20th century, physicist Leo Szilard helped resolve Maxwell’s Demon by proving that acquiring information inherently requires an expenditure of energy to reduce the entropy of a system .
Entropy is a measure of the disorder or randomness of a system . Think of flipping 30 water bottles. If all 30 land perfectly upside down on their caps, that is a highly ordered, very low entropy system . If they land randomly scattered, that is a highly disordered, high entropy system (which is statistically far more likely) .
Because the scattered bottles are the natural, likely state, it requires physical energy to organize them into the unlikely state of standing on their caps .
The information contained in our flashlight signal arises from intentionally arranging the flashes against random chance . Storing or communicating information explicitly requires forcing a system into a lower entropy state. The bits are simply the mathematical way we measure and represent that ordered state .

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
Introduction to Logic Gates
Why does the physics of information matter for programming? Because it allows us to build logic .
Imagine a simple light switch with two positions: Off (0) and On (1) . We establish a rule: If the light is on, you dance. If it is off, you do not dance .

Input 1 (Switch On): Light is on. You dance. 
Input 0 (Switch Off): Light is off. You do not dance. 

Now, we introduce a hardware component that intercepts and reverses the electrical signal. When the switch is On (1), it forces the light Off (0).

Input 1 (Switch On): Light is forced Off. You do not dance. 
Input 0 (Switch Off): Light is forced On. You dance. 

This type of signal manipulation is called a Gate . Specifically, this is a NOT Gate because it outputs the exact opposite of its input .
Let’s try a more complex logical rule using two switches. We construct the circuit so the light only turns on if BOTH switches are flipped On (1, 1) .

0, 0 \(\rightarrow\) Light Off (No dance) 
1, 0 \(\rightarrow\) Light Off (No dance) 
0, 1 \(\rightarrow\) Light Off (No dance) 
1, 1 \(\rightarrow\) Light On (Dance!) 

This is an AND Gate .
By combining millions of physical NOT, AND, and OR gates on a silicon chip, we create modern computers . Programming languages were invented simply as a human-readable way to manipulate these logic gates . Code isn’t magic; it is a rigid, physical system of organized logic .

title: The Basics: How Computers Work
text:
Memory and Processing
If information is a physical quantity, how do we store it? In our flashlight example, the information vanished the moment the light turned off .
To store information permanently, you need a physical container to hold the system in its low-entropy state so you can leave and come back to it later . This is called memory .

RAM (Random Access Memory): Very fast, temporary memory used by your computer to hold the data it is actively thinking about. When power is lost, the data is lost .
HDD (Hard Disk Drive): Older, slower storage that uses a magnetic arm to literally write bits onto a spinning metal platter .
SSD (Solid State Drive): Fast, modern storage with no moving parts . Instead of magnets, it relies on microscopic components called floating-gate transistors to physically trap electrons in a specific pattern, holding onto the data even when the computer is turned off.


CPU vs. GPU
To execute the logic gates and move this memory around, computers rely on processors .
The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is incredibly fast at doing single tasks in a sequential order . If you want to teach a computer to do a kickflip, the CPU learns step-by-step: first what a skateboard is, then how to ride it, then how to ollie, and finally how to kickflip . If it were painting a picture, the CPU is one master artist painting the entire canvas at lightning speed with a single brush .
The GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) is slower at single tasks, but excels at parallel processing—doing thousands of calculations at the exact same time . If the GPU were painting the same picture, it is like 5,000 artists painting one dot simultaneously . The GPU is much faster at rendering the final image, but it relies on the CPU to tell it what picture it is supposed to be painting in the first place.

title: What is a Programming Language?
text:
Think of writing code as providing an explicit set of instructions to a computer. The programming language is an interpreter that takes the code and translates it into something that the computer can understand. A programming language, in many ways, is exactly that—a language. It has its own syntax, grammar, and vocabulary.
Let’s say you speak English, but you want to communicate with someone who speaks Chinese. In order to communicate, there needs to be some way for the two of you to understand each other. One possibility is for you to simply learn Chinese so well that you can communicate whatever you need to. This kind of approach can take a very long time and requires quite a bit of study. To talk to a computer like this, instead of learning Chinese, you would essentially be learning how to flip bits on and off and speak in binary. Binary has its own structure that is very different from most spoken and written languages and can provide an even greater challenge to learn.
Instead of learning Chinese to communicate, you can find someone who already speaks Chinese and ask them to translate for you. The problem is, this translator doesn’t understand English perfectly; they understand it in a way that is very literal and basic. The translator also has no mind of their own to read between the lines or understand connotations or implications. In order to communicate, you need to be very exact with the words you choose to say to the translator.
It might be helpful to think of a programming language as a child that is only capable of doing things that you teach it to do. Want it to know what a banana is? You need to TEACH it what a banana is. Want it to understand how to write its name? You need to TEACH it to write its name. Want it to solve a complicated problem? You need to TEACH it HOW to solve the problem. The advantage of languages like Python is that other people have often figured out how to teach the language to do some very useful things, and you can utilize what other people have done. I’m not going to spend my time telling the code, in its language, how to compute a logarithm; I’m simply going to import the NumPy package because somebody else has already done that.
Let’s see how it might work telling this computer translator to “make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich.”
The translator will attempt to recognize each word because it can only translate literally:
The translator breaks. It doesn’t know what to do because it does not know what a “sandwich” is. If programmed properly, the translator will throw an error: “Error: I don’t know what ‘sandwich’ is.” This is the translator’s way of saying: “If you want your statement translated, you need to explicitly define what a ‘sandwich’ is first.”
Now, we have to figure out a way to define a sandwich in terms the translator can understand. We can try telling it something like: “‘sandwich’ = food between 2 slices of bread”.
The translator will now attempt to process this new definition:
Now you can attempt to run the original statement again: “make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich”
Python, C++, Fortran, etc., are all simply translators. They each have their own specific syntax and rules connected to very specific computer translations. You can only work within the framework of these computer/human translations.
